The Story of Virvati

I bow to Lord Jinendra, the friend of the world, the embodiment of purity, and the bestower of liberation's freedom, and I write the story of Virvati, which increases renunciation in the hearts of the noble.

In Rajgriha lived a merchant named Dhanmitra, whose wife was Dharini and whose son was Datt. In another city called Bhumigriha lived a householder named Anand, whose wife was Mitrvati. They had a daughter named Virvati. Virvati was married to Datt. As the saying goes, no one can prevent a match ordained by destiny.

In that same city lived a thief named Garak. Once, Virvati saw him and became captivated by his beauty. She began an illicit affair with him. Some time later, Datt set out for home after earning wealth on Ratnadvip. On the way lay his father-in-law's town, and since he had not seen his beloved wife in a long time and loved her dearly, he decided to visit her before going home. He stopped in a forest along the route, where a thief named Sahasrabhat spotted him. As Datt moved on, the thief followed him for amusement and accompanied him all the way to Bhumigriha.

At his in-laws' house, Datt was welcomed with great honour. Virvati too greeted him with affection, but her mind was not truly happy — it carried the mark of some deep wound. A clever man could have read her troubled countenance at once, but simple-hearted Datt detected nothing, for he could never suspect his wife of such a thing.

The truth was that the thief Garak, with whom Virvati was having an affair, was to be hanged that very day for some grave crime. Virvati was deeply distressed by this, and her mind was in turmoil. At night, when everyone in the house was asleep, Virvati rose alone, took a sword in her hand, and headed toward the execution ground. The thief Sahasrabhat, who had followed Datt, saw her leaving and followed her to see where she was going in the dead of night. Hearing footsteps behind her, Virvati turned and struck blindly with her sword, killing the follower — not knowing it was Sahasrabhat and not her beloved Garak.

Meanwhile, Garak was executed by the king's men as scheduled. Virvati returned home to find her husband Datt still asleep, and she lay down beside him as if nothing had happened. But by morning, the body of Sahasrabhat was discovered, and the investigation led back to Virvati. Her crime was exposed — her affair with a condemned criminal, her midnight excursion, and her killing of an innocent man in the dark.

Datt was heartbroken. The woman he had loved and trusted had not only betrayed him but had taken an innocent life. He renounced all worldly attachment, became a monk, and through dedicated spiritual practice, eventually attained liberation.

This story teaches that infidelity breeds only destruction — not only for the unfaithful one but for everyone around them. Trust once broken can never be fully restored, and the web of deceit entangles more lives than the sinner ever imagined. Datt, the innocent husband, found in his suffering the doorway to renunciation and ultimate freedom.
